summary: This Informational document lists functional requirements for operations, administration, and maintenance mechanisms, protocols, and tools in the Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) layer.

eli5.summary: A checklist of things a repair crew needs in order to check and fix a multicast delivery system.

subtitle: What operations teams need to monitor and manage a BIER multicast network

tldr.problem: BIER is a new way to send data to multiple destinations efficiently, but operators need tools to monitor, troubleshoot, and maintain these networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists 18 functional requirements for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanisms that BIER networks must support, including monitoring tools, fault detection, and performance measurement.
tldr.outcome: BIER implementations can now design OAM features that meet these standard requirements, allowing operators to keep multicast networks healthy and responsive.

today: RFC 9974 is an Informational RFC listing the consensus requirements of the IETF for BIER OAM solutions. It has not been obsoleted and provides guidance for vendors implementing BIER support and operators deploying BIER networks.

sections.title: What BIER Is and Why OAM Matters
sections.content:
BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication), defined in RFC 8279, is an architecture for multicast—sending the same data to many receivers efficiently. Unlike traditional multicast, BIER uses a bitmap where each bit represents a destination; the sender lists which destinations should receive a copy by setting the corresponding bits.

This document does not define new OAM protocols. Instead, it lists the functional requirements that any OAM solution must meet to support BIER networks. Operations teams use OAM tools to monitor path health, measure performance, detect faults, and verify connectivity—the same way network operators use tools to check traditional IP networks.
sections.eli5: BIER is a clever way to send a message to multiple people at once. But how do you check if the message got there? This document lists what checks you need to be able to do.

sections.title: The 18 OAM Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements fall into several categories. Session management: OAM sessions must be startable from any router in the BIER domain, or from a controller. Sessions can be proactive (continuous monitoring) or on-demand (manual diagnostics). Monitoring methods: Both active (inject test packets) and passive (observe live traffic) monitoring must work. Path continuity checking: An operator must be able to verify that a multicast path to each egress router is reachable and has no breaks.

Performance measurement: OAM must calculate metrics like packet loss, delay, and delay variation over the multicast tree. Bidirectional monitoring: In the forward direction, OAM packets must travel the same path as monitored data (including QoS treatment); in the reverse, they may take a different route. Special features: Path MTU discovery, remote defect indication (RDI—a signal that something is wrong), defect notifications, and fault messages between routers all must be supported.

The document names existing protocols as examples (BFD, STAMP, Alternate-Marking) but does not require them. It also requires that OAM solutions protect the control plane from flooding attacks when test packets are replicated across the multicast tree.
sections.eli5: The requirements cover: starting health checks, checking if packages arrived, measuring how fast they traveled, finding broken links, and warning other routers when something is wrong. All in a way that doesn't break the network from too many test messages.

sections.title: What This Covers and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The requirements apply to any routing underlay (IP, MPLS, or others) that BIER might run on top of. They are mandatory for implementations that claim to support BIER OAM—not merely optional nice-to-haves. The document lists what must work but not how to build it; the actual protocols and tools are defined elsewhere.

This is an informational document, so it does not set IETF standards, only the consensus view of what operators need. The document does not cover how to manage the BIER control plane itself (how routers learn the domain and set up forwarding state), only how to monitor and maintain the forwarding paths once they exist.
sections.eli5: This is a to-do list, not a how-to guide. It says what must work but not which tools to use.

sections.title: Security of OAM in Multicast
sections.content:
One security risk in multicast OAM is amplification: if an operator sends one test packet and the multicast tree copies it to 1,000 egress routers, those routers might each send a reply, creating 1,000 responses to one request. This can be used as a denial-of-service attack. The requirements mandate that BIER OAM solutions must control the rate at which test packets are sent and limit the number of OAM messages sent to the control plane. Implementations should carefully manage where and how echo replies are sent.

The requirements inherit security considerations from RFC 8279 (BIER) and RFC 8296 (BIER encapsulation). Operators should use standard network security practices: access control, authentication, and authorization for who can start OAM sessions.
sections.eli5: If a bad actor sends many test messages, the multicast tree could multiply them into millions of replies that overwhelm the network. The solution is to rate-limit test messages and replies.

sections.title: What This Means for Operators and Implementers
sections.content:
For equipment vendors building BIER support, these requirements define the OAM features that production networks will expect. Operators can use this document as a checklist when evaluating BIER implementations: does the vendor's OAM support include proactive and on-demand monitoring, performance metrics, fault detection, and RDI signaling?

The document was written by consensus of the IETF community and approved by the Internet Engineering Steering Group, but as an informational RFC, it does not define any new protocols or IANA registrations. Its value is in documenting the shared expectations of the network operations community about what a mature BIER implementation should support.
sections.eli5: This tells equipment makers what operators will need, and tells operators what to look for when choosing BIER equipment.

items.title: Monitoring
items.text: Proactive (continuous) and on-demand (manual) monitoring of multicast paths.

items.title: Path Continuity
items.text: Verify each egress is reachable and the path has no breaks.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Measure loss, delay, and delay variation over the multicast tree.

items.title: Fault Detection
items.text: Signal problems with remote defect indication (RDI) and alerts.

items.title: Bidirectional
items.text: Forward path matches the data flow; reverse path can differ.

items.title: Protection
items.text: Control plane protection against OAM message flooding.
